python.name: Python
python.tagline: Reads like English, runs half the modern world.
python.what: Python is a general-purpose programming language designed to be readable first. That single decision is why it became the default language of data science, automation, machine learning and backend services alike — you spend your effort on the problem instead of on the syntax.
why: The gentlest entry into programming that still leads to a serious career — nothing is a toy language you outgrow.
One language covers web backends, data analysis, automation and AI, so your second project reuses the skills from your first.
The largest package ecosystem in software: whatever you need to do, a well-tested library already does most of it.
Consistently among the most in-demand languages in job listings, and the standard language of AI research.

build.title: An automation bot
build.desc: Turn a repetitive daily task into a script that runs by itself — file sorting, reports, scraping a site for changes.

build.title: A REST API
build.desc: A real backend with FastAPI: routes, a database, authentication, and documentation generated for you.

build.title: A data analysis
build.desc: Take a messy real-world dataset, clean it, and produce charts that actually answer a question.

roadmap.detail: Syntax, data types, control flow, functions. Writing programs that do something on day one.
Files, modules, error handling, and object-oriented design — how code stays readable past 100 lines.
Virtual environments, pip, requests, pandas. Standing on other people's work properly.
A database-backed API, tests, Git, and deployment. The parts that separate a script from a product.

javascript.name: JavaScript
javascript.tagline: The only language that runs natively in every browser on earth.
javascript.what: JavaScript is the language of the web. It is the only one browsers execute directly, which means every interactive page you have ever used runs it. With Node.js it also runs on servers, and with TypeScript it gains the type safety that makes large codebases survivable.
why: Non-negotiable for web work — there is no alternative that runs in the browser without compiling to it.
One language for the whole stack: the same skills drive the interface, the server and the build tooling.
TypeScript turns it into a language you can build something large in without fear of refactoring.
The largest hiring market of any language, and the easiest to freelance in.

build.title: An interactive interface
build.desc: DOM manipulation, events and state — a page that responds instead of just displaying.

build.title: A app that talks to an API
build.desc: Fetch, async/await, error and loading states. The shape of every real front end.

build.title: A typed codebase
build.desc: The same project rewritten in TypeScript, where the compiler catches your mistakes before users do.

roadmap.detail: Types, functions, scope, closures. Understanding what actually happens, not memorising patterns.
DOM, events, forms, storage — making a page react to a person.
Promises, async/await, fetch. Working with a network that is slow and sometimes fails.
Types, generics, modules, bundlers. Code that scales past one file and one author.

flutter.name: Flutter
flutter.tagline: One codebase, running on both phones in your pocket.
flutter.what: Flutter is Google's toolkit for building applications from a single codebase that run natively on both Android and iOS — and on the web and desktop from that same source. It draws every pixel itself instead of wrapping each platform's own widgets, which is why a Flutter app looks and behaves identically on both phones rather than quietly drifting apart.
why: Two app stores from one codebase — the single largest saving in mobile development, and the reason small teams reach for it.
Mobile is where clients in this region actually spend their budget: delivery, banking, booking and logistics apps all need it.
Dart comes easily after Python or JavaScript — you are learning a framework, not fighting an unfamiliar language.
Hot reload puts your change on a real device in under a second, which makes learning interface work genuinely fast.

build.title: A multi-screen app
build.desc: Navigation, forms and local storage, running on a real handset from the first week.

build.title: An app backed by an API
build.desc: Sign-in, network calls, honest loading and error states, and offline caching.

build.title: A published release
build.desc: Icons, splash screen, signing keys and a build submitted to the Play Store.

roadmap.detail: Syntax, types, async and null safety, practised on small console programs.
Composition, state, navigation and layouts that survive a rotation.
REST calls, state management, persistence and testing.
Native integrations, performance profiling, store assets and release.

frontend.name: Frontend
frontend.tagline: Where design becomes something people can actually use.
frontend.what: Frontend development is the craft of building the part of a product people touch. Modern frontend means React and Next.js for structure, Tailwind for styling, and a real concern for performance and accessibility — because an interface that is beautiful but slow or unusable has failed.
why: The most visible work in software: you can show your portfolio to anyone, technical or not.
The clearest path from beginner to employed — junior frontend roles are the most common entry point in the industry.
Immediate feedback. You change a line and see it, which makes learning far faster than backend work.
Highly freelance-friendly: small businesses need sites and are willing to pay individuals for them.

build.title: A responsive marketing site
build.desc: Pixel-accurate from a design, working from a phone to a wide monitor.

build.title: A dashboard
build.desc: Components, routing, data fetching, and state that stays correct as the app grows.

build.title: A production Next.js app
build.desc: Server rendering, image optimisation, SEO metadata and a real deployment.

roadmap.detail: Semantics, flexbox, grid, responsive design. The foundation most self-taught developers skip and regret.
Components, props, state, hooks. Thinking in composable pieces rather than pages.
Routing, server components, data loading, rendering strategies and SEO.
Accessibility, performance budgets, animation and design systems — what makes work look professional.

vibe.name: Vibe Coding
vibe.tagline: Building with AI as a collaborator, not an autocomplete.
vibe.what: Vibe coding is the practice of building software with AI assistants as a genuine part of the workflow — describing intent, reviewing what comes back, and iterating quickly. It is a real skill: knowing how to specify, how to verify, and where the assistant is confidently wrong is what separates a fast developer from a dangerous one.
why: It is already how a large share of professional development is done — this is current practice, not a prediction.
It compresses the time from idea to working prototype dramatically.
It lowers the barrier into programming without lowering the ceiling.
The judgement it demands — reading code critically, testing claims — makes you a better engineer regardless of the tools.

build.title: A prototype in a day
build.desc: Idea to deployed, working application in a single session, with AI carrying the boilerplate.

build.title: A verified feature
build.desc: Adding to an existing codebase with AI, then proving it works — the discipline most people skip.

build.title: Your own workflow
build.desc: Prompts, rules and tooling tuned to how you build, so the speed persists after the course.

roadmap.detail: Modern AI coding assistants, what each is good at, and how to drive them.
Describing intent precisely enough to get useful output — the core skill.
Reading generated code critically, testing it, and catching confident mistakes.
Taking an AI-built prototype all the way to something real people can use safely.
